analysis.one_liner: Closes a Clean Air Act loophole so oil and gas wells and pipelines can be regulated for toxic air emissions.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or vote, after 47 Democrats plus the sponsor backed it and no Republicans did.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have removed a Clean Air Act exemption that keeps emissions from thousands of oil and gas wells, pipeline compressors, and pump stations from being counted together when the EPA decides whether a facility is a "major source" of toxic air pollution. With the emissions aggregated, the EPA could impose stricter toxic-emission controls on those operations. It also would have required the EPA to add hydrogen sulfide, a poisonous gas released in oil and gas production, to its official list of hazardous air pollutants within 180 days, and to set pollution rules for the sources that emit it.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or attend school near oil and gas wells, compressor stations, and pipelines would gain, because their air would be subject to toxic-emission controls that the current aggregation exemption shields those facilities from. Workers in nearby communities and the public at large would benefit from EPA rules covering hydrogen sulfide, which the bill directs the agency to regulate for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near oil and gas wells

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Clean Air Act provision that exempts oil and gas wells and pipeline compressor and pump stations from having their emissions aggregated, so their combined pollution could be regulated as a major source of hazardous air pollutants under section 112 of the Act.

Requires the EPA to add hydrogen sulfide to the list of hazardous air pollutants within 180 days of enactment, and to set emission standards for its major and area sources, including oil and gas wells, within a year after that.

Allows emissions from oil and gas production wells to be regulated as an area source of toxic air pollutants, extending controls to smaller clusters of wells that today fall outside major-source rules.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and pipeline operators would bear new compliance costs: once emissions from scattered wells and compressor stations are added together, many operations would cross the "major source" threshold and face stricter emission standards, permits, and controls. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers through energy prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and pipeline operators

drawbacks.text: Aggregating emissions from dispersed wells and pipeline stations could sweep many small operators into major-source permitting, imposing significant compliance costs that could raise production costs and energy prices.

The bill sets hard deadlines (180 days for the hydrogen sulfide rule, 365 days for listing source categories) rather than letting the EPA's usual rulemaking process set the pace, which leaves little time for the scientific review and public comment those rules normally require.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health gain is real but localized: stricter air-toxics controls matter most to people living near well fields, compressor stations, and pipelines. The costs fall on a specific industry and are real but standard for air-pollution regulation — the same kind of compliance burden other industrial sources have carried under the Clean Air Act for decades. The bill was a straightforward regulatory fix rather than a badly designed one, though its rigid deadlines would have squeezed the EPA's rulemaking timeline. It never advanced far enough for the tradeoff to be tested in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, passed down to the environment subcommittee a week later, and nothing further ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Yvette Clarke introduced the bill on January 16, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

Nine days later, on January 25, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change, where the action history ends — no hearing, no markup, no vote is recorded for the remainder of the 116th Congress.
The bill attracted 47 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans, and never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and pipeline operators came out ahead: because the bill never left subcommittee, the aggregation exemption stayed in place and their wells and pipeline stations remained shielded from major-source toxic-emission regulation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers and pipeline operators

for.name: 47 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill the day it was introduced and never reported it out; no hearing or markup appears in the action history for the rest of the Congress.

against.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change

sides.party_line_note: All 48 backers were Democrats (the sponsor plus 47 cosponsors) with no Republican support, and the Democratic-controlled committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill removes the statutory exemption that keeps emissions from oil and gas wells from being added together and regulated as a major source of toxic air pollution, exposing well operators to stricter emission standards and permitting. Hydrogen sulfide — a toxic gas released in production — would become a regulated hazardous air pollutant with rules covering oil and gas wells.
Emissions from pipeline compressor stations and pump stations, currently exempt from aggregation, would be counted with other sources and could trigger major-source controls for the first time.
